triples.relationship: Learned instruction passed on for others' benefit
triples.rationale: Sirach's translator says lovers of learning should benefit others by speaking and writing, before describing his grandfather's reading. Timothy is instructed to entrust what he heard to faithful people able to teach others. Both make reception of teaching lead to communicating it onward; neither the grandfather Jesus nor the translator is identified with anyone in Timothy.
triples.source_text: but lovers of learning should also be able to benefit those outside, both by speaking and by writing, my grandfather Jesus, having devoted himself extensively to reading the law and the prophets

target_units.text: and the things you heard from me through many witnesses, entrust these to faithful people who will be able to teach others also.

triples.relationship: Sleepless literary labor undertaken for readers
triples.rationale: Sirach's translator reports wakeful hours, skill and hard work to translate and publish for learners abroad. The Maccabees abridger describes sweat and sleeplessness while undertaking difficult literary labor for readers' benefit. The particular parallel is labor and lost sleep to make a work useful to others; translation and abridgment remain distinct tasks and authors.
triples.source_text: I myself considered it most necessary to contribute some diligence and hard work toward translating this book. During that time I devoted many wakeful hours and much skill to completing the book and publishing it also for those living abroad who wish to learn,

target_units.text: we have taken thought for the pleasure of those who wish to read, for the ease of those eager to commit it to memory, and for the benefit of everyone who encounters it.
For us who have undertaken the hard work of abridgement, the task is not easy; it involves sweat and sleeplessness.
Just as it is not easy for someone preparing a banquet and seeking others’ benefit, nevertheless, for the gratitude of the many, we will gladly bear the hard work.

triples.relationship: An opponent lying in wait for one's words
triples.rationale: Sirach warns that an insolent person may ambush the hearer's mouth when opposed. After the rebuke of the law experts, Luke describes scribes and Pharisees lying in wait to catch something from Jesus' mouth. The shared ambush-against-speech image is explicit; the narrative does not make Jesus' rebuke a moral fault or identify a single opponent as Sirach's individual.
triples.source_text: Do not rise up against an insolent person, lest he sit in ambush against your mouth.

target_units.text: Woe to you experts in the Law, because you have taken away the key of knowledge! You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.”
When He went out from there, the scribes and Pharisees began to press Him fiercely and question Him closely about many things,
lying in wait for Him to catch something from His mouth.

triples.relationship: Apparently friendly questioning used as a test
triples.rationale: Sirach warns that a powerful person's many words and smiling examination can be a test. Matthew's plot to trap Jesus begins with praise of His truthfulness before a question, which Jesus identifies as testing with evil intent. Both expose outwardly favorable conversation serving a hostile examination; Matthew does not explicitly describe a smile or an attempt to converse as an equal.
triples.source_text: Do not insist on speaking with him as an equal, and do not trust his many words. For through much talk he will test you and examine you as though smiling.

target_units.text: Then the Pharisees went and took counsel how to trap Him in a statement.

They sent Him their disciples with the Herodians, saying, “Teacher, we know that Thou art truthful and dost teach God’s way in truth. Thou art not swayed by anyone, for Thou dost not look at people’s outward status.
Tell us, then, what Thou thinkest: is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not?”
Knowing their evil intent, Jesus said, “Why do you test Me, hypocrites?

triples.rationale: Sirach promises measured instruction and precise knowledge. Ecclesiastes is described as teaching knowledge, with an ear tracing an orderly arrangement of proverbs and a search for delightful, upright, truthful words. Both associate wisdom teaching with care in its expression and order; the target's wording about an ear is preserved rather than assigning it an unstated editorial action.
triples.source_text: I will disclose instruction by measure and declare knowledge with precision.

target_units.text: Besides becoming wise, Ecclesiastes also taught the people knowledge; and an ear will trace out an orderly arrangement of proverbs.
Ecclesiastes sought much to find words of delight and something written in uprightness, words of truth.

triples.relationship: A pierced heart producing an expressed response
triples.rationale: Sirach says pricking a heart reveals feeling, paired with an eye prick producing tears. Acts describes hearers pierced to the heart who immediately ask what they should do. The shared image makes an inward piercing lead to a visible verbal response; Acts supplies a particular repentance setting, without making that the meaning of every heart-pricking in Sirach.
triples.source_text: The one who pricks an eye will bring down tears; the one who pricks a heart reveals feeling.

target_units.text: When they heard this, they were pierced to the heart and said to Peter and the other apostles, “Men, brothers, what should we do?”

triples.rationale: Sirach's dependent guest supplies entertainment and drink but receives no thanks and hears bitter words. Luke's household slave is ordered to serve food and drink, followed by the question whether the master thanks him for obeying. Both portray table service without gratitude, while a guest's humiliating dependence differs from a slave's stated duty; Luke does not include Sirach's bitter insults.
triples.source_text: You will entertain and provide drink without thanks, and besides these things you will hear bitter words:

target_units.text: Will he not instead say to him, ‘Prepare something for my supper, gird yourself, and serve me while I eat and drink; and after that you shall eat and drink’?
Does he thank the slave because he did what was commanded?

triples.relationship: A dependent person ordered to prepare another's meal
triples.rationale: Sirach quotes a host ordering his guest to arrange the table and feed him from what he has. Luke quotes a master's instruction to prepare supper and serve while the master eats and drinks. The parallel is the command making a dependent person provide the meal; the guest and slave are distinct statuses, and Luke does not demand the servant's own possessions.
triples.source_text: “Come along, guest, arrange the table, and if you have anything in your hand, feed me.

target_units.text: Will he not instead say to him, ‘Prepare something for my supper, gird yourself, and serve me while I eat and drink; and after that you shall eat and drink’?

triples.rationale: Sirach ranks health and a robust body above gold and immeasurable wealth. In Job, the devil claims that a person will pay whatever he has for his life, then proposes touching Job's bones and flesh. Both statements place bodily welfare above possessions. The target claim belongs to the devil's accusation and is not made a divine endorsement or equated with Sirach's whole teaching.
triples.source_text: Health and soundness are better than all gold, and a robust body than immeasurable wealth.

target_units.text: The devil replied to the Lord, “Skin for skin! Whatever a person has, he will pay for his life.
But indeed, stretch out Thy hand and touch his bones and his flesh; surely he will curse Thee to Thy face.”

triples.relationship: A servant's labor supplying the master's ease
triples.rationale: Sirach tells the owner to put a servant to work to find rest. Luke depicts a master requiring further meal preparation and service after a slave's fieldwork so that the master may eat and drink first. Both describe the master's benefit from assigned servant labor; Luke does not state the source's warning that released hands lead to seeking freedom.
triples.source_text: Make a servant work, and you will find rest; release his hands, and he will seek freedom.

target_units.text: Which of you, having a slave plowing or tending sheep, will say to him when he comes in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’?
Will he not instead say to him, ‘Prepare something for my supper, gird yourself, and serve me while I eat and drink; and after that you shall eat and drink’?

triples.relationship: Freedom from pressing activity allowing attentive learning
triples.rationale: Sirach connects a scribe's opportunity for wisdom with leisure and reduced activity. Mary sits listening to the Lord while Martha is distracted by much serving, and Mary's chosen portion is affirmed. Both place attentive learning alongside relief from competing work; the narrative does not identify Mary as a scribe or issue Sirach's general claim about every worker.
triples.source_text: A scribe’s wisdom comes through the opportunity of leisure; the one whose activity is reduced will become wise.

target_units.text: She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to His word.
But Martha was distracted by much serving. She came up and said, “Lord, dost Thou not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, then, to help me.”
The Lord answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed; for Mary has chosen the good portion, which shall not be taken from her.”

triples.relationship: Inner fullness expressed as a need to speak further
triples.rationale: Sirach's teacher will recount more because he has become full like the midmonth moon. Elihu will speak again because he is full of words, likening his belly to fermenting wine in a tied skin and a burst bellows. Both use fullness imagery to introduce further speech, while the moon and wine/bellows images and their speakers remain distinct.
triples.source_text: Having reflected further, I will recount more, for I have become full like the moon at midmonth.

target_units.text: “I will speak again, for I am full of words; the spirit of my belly is destroying me.
My belly is like a tied wineskin of fermenting new wine, or like a smith’s bellows that has burst.
I will speak so that I may rest, opening my lips.

deferred_source_units.source_text: There is someone who grows rich through his attention and frugality, and this is his allotted reward:
deferred_source_units.reason: The native Proverbs 13:11 contrasts lawless acquisition with gathering in piety. It does not state Sirach's attention-and-frugality method. The distinct moral and economic descriptions are not treated as the same specific reason for growing rich.

deferred_source_units.source_text: There is someone who makes a promise to a friend because of shame, and has acquired him as an enemy for nothing.
deferred_source_units.reason: Matthew 14:7-9 says Herod promised with an oath after the dance and later acted because of the oaths and guests. It neither calls the recipient his friend nor describes her becoming his enemy through the promise, and does not say shame caused the original promise. The particular causal sequence in Sirach remains unmatched.

target_units.text: Therefore he promised with an oath to give her whatever she asked.
Prompted by her mother, she said, “Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptist.”
Although the king was grieved, because of his oaths and those reclining with him, he ordered it to be given.
